capsid #936 repinned the Portal to Capsomer 0.145.0. Capsomer 0.139 had moved `.cap-stack`, `.cap-cluster`, `.cap-panes` and `.cap-text` out of `base.css` into `layout.css` and `text.css`, and the Portal imported neither, so the live Portal lost its layout and no check noticed. This makes a repin like that fail.

**Where.** I put it in `devkit-css-vars`, not in a new bin. It is the same kind of gate: a CSS reference that resolves to nothing. It also uses the same walk, comment handling and `.css-vars.json`, and `pr.yml` already runs it in every repository with that file, so no workflow input is needed. Capsomer's own CLI warns and exits 0 (its rulings), so the failing gate goes here.

**What it checks.** `.css-vars.json` takes an optional `classes` list, for example `[{ "package": "dashboard/node_modules/capsomer", "dirs": ["dashboard/src"], "prefix": "cap-" }]`.
- The package's stylesheets are its `exports` ending in `.css`, `*` patterns included, plus the files those `@import`.
- A stylesheet styles a class when the class is in the first compound of one of its top-level selectors. That covers `:is(.cap-stack, .cap-grid)[data-gap]`, but not a class after a combinator, inside `:not()`/`:has()`, or in a nested rule.
- What the site loads is every `"capsomer/<x>.css"` its files name, followed through the package's own imports.
- The check fails on a class that a `.ts`/`.tsx` file writes, that the package styles, and that no loaded stylesheet styles. It reports the class once, at its first use, and names the stylesheets that would load it.

**The map.** The class-to-stylesheet map is read from the installed package itself (its export map and its CSS) on every run, so it can never drift from the pinned Capsomer. Capsomer needs no generated file.

**Proved on capsid.** On the Portal with `layout.css`/`text.css` removed from `root.tsx` (the state #936 shipped), it fails with:
```

dashboard/src/app/ConfirmDialog.tsx:228: .cap-text is styled in capsomer/text-role.css, which nothing here imports
```

author: arthurcsoncini09-collab
body:
## O que muda
O Terminal Lab virou **três terminais em abas**:
- **CMD:** Prompt de Comando do Windows.
- **PowerShell:** Windows PowerShell 5.1.
- **Bash:** Ubuntu 24.04.

Cada um tem o visual, o prompt, as opções e as mensagens de erro do terminal de verdade.

### Rede virtual que reage
- O computador do aluno (192.168.1.37), o roteador, um servidor, uma impressora e sites conhecidos estão na mesma rede simulada. Qualquer outro domínio válido também resolve.
- `ipconfig /release` ou `sudo dhclient -r` tira o IP: o ping dá "Falha geral" e o DNS para. `/renew` ou `dhclient` devolve o IP, mostrando o DORA.
- Fazer ping num host local o coloca na tabela ARP. Consultas ao DNS enchem o cache (`ipconfig /displaydns`, `Get-DnsClientCache`).
- Hosts inexistentes, redes sem rota e portas fechadas dão o erro certo de cada sistema.

### Comandos (170 implementados, fora os apelidos)
- **CMD:** `ipconfig` (/all /release /renew /flushdns /displaydns), `ping`, `tracert`, `pathping`, `nslookup`, `arp`, `netstat`, `route`, `getmac`, `netsh`, `curl`, `dir`, `cd`, `type`, `md`, `rd`, `del`, `copy`, `move`, `ren`, `tree`, `find`, `findstr`, `sort`, `set`, `systeminfo`, `tasklist`…
- **PowerShell:** `Get-NetIPConfiguration`, `Get-NetIPAddress`, `Get-NetAdapter`, `Get-NetRoute`, `Get-NetNeighbor`, `Get-NetTCPConnection`, `Resolve-DnsName`, `Test-Connection`, `Test-NetConnection` (-Port, -TraceRoute), `Invoke-WebRequest`, `Invoke-RestMethod`, `Get-ChildItem`, `Get-Content`, `New-Item`, `Select-String`, `Select-Object`, `Where-Object`, `$PSVersionTable`, `$env:`… e os programas do Windows. `curl` é apelido do `Invoke-WebRequest`, como no 5.1, e o terminal explica isso.
- **Bash:** `ip a/r/link/neigh`, `ifconfig`, `ping -c`, `traceroute`, `tracepath`, `dig`, `host`, `nslookup`, `ss`, `netstat`, `arp`, `route`, `curl`, `wget`, `nc -zv`, `nmap`, `dhclient`, `nmcli`, `resolvectl`, `ufw`, `iptables`, `ssh`, `telnet`, `ls`, `cd`, `cat`, `grep`, `head`, `tail`, `wc`, `find`, `tree`, `sudo`…

### Uso
- Pipes (`|`), `>` e `>>`, `&&` e `;`, variáveis (`%USERNAME%`, `$env:USERNAME`, `$HOME`, `$?`).
- **↑/↓** navegam no histórico, **Tab** completa comandos e caminhos e **Ctrl+L** limpa a tela.
- Lista lateral clicável, quadro "O que aconteceu" com a explicação do último comando e tabela **"o mesmo comando nos três terminais"**.
- CMD e PowerShell dividem os mesmos arquivos e a mesma rede (é o mesmo PC).

## Testado
- `tsc`, `next lint` e `npm run build` ok.
- Script roda os 121 comandos dos catálogos e cerca de 100 casos de erro e de mudança de estado nos 3 shells, com 0 falhas.
- No navegador: digitação, Tab, histórico, cliques na lista e na tabela, as 3 abas e o celular, sem erros no console.

author: jlevy
body:
Bead `mb-0zil`. The Pulls tab’s Open, Closed, and All lists have no total cap. They load
incrementally as the reader scrolls, as Commits does, and show the file scan’s progress
indicator in place of count notices.

## Where the cap was

The server catalog never had a total cap. `refresh_pull_list` already backfilled every
pull request (`test_backfill_all_beyond_old_cap…`). The cap a reader saw came from the
panel:

- `DISPLAY_ROWS = 500` and its “Showing last 500” notice.
- Each approach to the tail added one 100-row page (“Showing last 600”).
- Past the cached rows the list just stopped, under “Showing last N” and **Fetch more**,
  with no sign that more were coming.

I reproduced this in headless Chrome against a fake `gh` that answers in 1.5 s a page.
The list sat at 500, then 600, then 700, with nothing at its foot.

## The change

- **Panel (`pulls-panel.js`):**
  - Removed “Showing last N”, “Catalog paused · N cached”, and **Fetch more**.
  - Each approach to the tail reads one more 100-row cache page, through the filter’s
    last row. A reader parked at the tail keeps reading as GitHub’s pages land.
  - The list’s foot shows progress with the nav’s scan indicator:
    `.index-progress-spinner` and `.index-progress-text`, the same classes the folder
    overview reuses, after `.mb-delayed-loading`’s 50 ms quiet period.
  - Its text is “~N pull requests fetched” while GitHub’s pages for this filter are
    arriving. It is “Fetching pull requests…” while a page is being read.
  - The indicator leaves with the last row.
- **Server (`pull_list_refresh.py`, `pull_list_route.py`):**
  - The backfill past the reader’s prefix is background work. Before each page it now
    asks `gh_budget.admission(("graphql",))`.
  - Below the floor, or under a rate hold, it stops at a page boundary without a failure
    stamp.
  - `POST pulls-refresh` starts no job for an ask whose prefix is already cached.
  - The reader’s own pages still run at any budget: the filter’s prefix as far as they
    scrolled, and the freshness scan.

## Measurements (2026-11-13)

- **Real catalog page:** `cli/cli` took 1.6–1.8 s and one GraphQL point a page (3
  pages). A 30,000-PR backfill is about 300 points, 6% of the hourly 5,000, over 8–9
  minutes. I set no new pacing bound.
- **Cache window:** 2 ms of server time at the top, middle, and end of a 30,000-row
  catalog. From Chrome it is 6–7 ms a page, so re-reading a changed 10,000-row prefix
  takes about 0.7 s. That number is recorded beside `WINDOW_ROWS`.

## Tests

Each new or changed test below fails on main and passes here, except the route paging
test, which passes on main.

- `tests/test_github_pull_list.py`:
  - Closed pages through every old cap (passes on main: the route had no cap).
  - The backfill pauses below the budget floor and resumes.
  - A rate hold pauses the backfill without a refusal of its own.
- `tests/dom/github-pulls-catalog-behavior.js`:
  - Scrolling through 2,500 rows with no count notice.
  - A parked tail fed by arriving pages, and progress text.
- `tests/dom/github-pulls-panel-session.js`: progress below the rows while a page is on
  its way, and no count notice anywhere.
- `cli-github-pulls-backfill.txt`: a new `metab --api` golden. It records the pause,
  scrolling past it, the resumption, and Closed paged past 1,000 rows. Its parity rows
  are in `arch-views-models-routes.md`.
- `make -o install lint-check`, including parity and goldens, passes. The GitHub Pulls
  pytest suites pass (571), and so do the GitHub and Pulls tryscript goldens.

Docs and CHANGELOG are updated. This branch merges #370, #406, and #407 from main; #407’s
numbered chips and Reload are kept.

author: drastixs
body:
## Summary

- Adds the LeRobot 0.7.0 calibration of the two SO-101 arms (`calibration/`). The folders have the LeRobot layout, so `HF_LEROBOT_CALIBRATION=<repo>/calibration` works directly.
- Adds the helper scripts used to calibrate the arms and start teleoperation (`tools/lerobot/`).

## Hardware change: leader servo IDs

The servo IDs of the leader arm were in reverse order (ID 1 was the gripper). Because of this, the leader calibration recorded about 360° for `shoulder_lift`, and teleoperation would send each joint to the wrong follower joint. The IDs were changed in the servo EEPROM to the LeRobot order (1 = `shoulder_pan` … 6 = `gripper`), and then the leader was calibrated again. `leader.json` is correct only for this ID order. `calibration/README.md` records this.

The follower IDs were already in the correct order.

## Scripts

All scripts only read the servos, except:

- `renumber_leader_ids.py`: writes the EEPROM. It was a one-time fix. It needs `--yes-reverse-ids`, because a second run would make the IDs wrong again.
- `teleop_aligned.py`: waits until the leader and follower poses are within 20°, then starts `lerobot-teleoperate` with a 30° step limit.

## Test

- Leader and follower ranges are 187–207° for each joint (`wrist_roll` full turn), and `gripper` is 132–134°.
- `compare_arms.py`: all joints move in the same direction on the two arms.
- `lerobot-teleoperate` ran with both arms connected.

author: mingyumaz
body:
## Summary

`SendNs3Packet()`, which puts the frames of the P4 core onto the ports, skipped port 511 with a bare number. This PR uses the constant `SSWITCH_DROP_PORT` there, as the cores and the PNA NIC already do, and says in a comment why the port is skipped. The behavior does not change. Target branch: `main`.

### How it should work
BMv2's simple_switch has a drop port: a packet whose `egress_spec` is the drop port at the end of the ingress or the egress is dropped. `mark_to_drop()` sets `egress_spec` to it. Its default is 511; `simple_switch --drop-port` can change it.

In p4sim the drop port is `SSWITCH_DROP_PORT` (511). `P4SwitchCore` keeps it as `m_dropPort`, and the v1model core compares `egress_spec` with it. No attribute changes it.

### What went wrong
Nothing that a simulation can see: `SendNs3Packet()` used the right value, but as the bare number 511. It means "the drop port": a frame for it is dropped without a warning, and a frame for any other port that does not exist is dropped with one. Frames for port 511 come from:
- the pipeline core (`P4SWITCH_ARCH_PIPELINE`), which passes the `egress_spec` of the ingress, so a frame marked with `mark_to_drop()` ends here;
- v1model, only for a multicast copy or a clone for port 511. BMv2 would send it to port 511, which does not exist, so it is dropped there too.

I also compared the rest of the v1model drop path with BMv2 1.15.8. At the start of the egress, BMv2 sets `egress_spec` to drop port + 1 (512), p4sim to 0. In the 9-bit field of v1model both become 0, so the P4 program sees the same value.

### The change
- `SendNs3Packet()` compares the port with the named drop port instead of 511.
- A comment says why a frame for the drop port is dropped without a warning.

### How the test works
There is no new test, because the behavior does not change. Even without this check, a frame for port 511 would be dropped by a switch with fewer than 512 ports, since that port does not exist; only the warning would differ.

### Code changes
- `model/p4-switch-net-device.cc`: `SendNs3Packet()` uses `SSWITCH_DROP_PORT`.

## Testing

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Build | no p4sim warnings |
| `format-utils`, `p4-topology-reader`, `p4-p2p-channel`, `p4-queue`, `p4sim`, `p4-controller`, `p4-packet` | all pass, run one at a time |
| Mutation test | not applicable: the behavior does not change |
| The 19 smoke examples of `examples-to-run.py`, before and after | identical output (wall-clock and Thrift port lines excluded) |

All BMv2 runs ran in a private `/tmp` and network namespace, so that simulations in another ns-3 tree could not interfere.

### Not in this PR
- **`drop` and `mark_to_drop`** still write the bare number 511 on main. #43 (clone and digest, stacked on #39) changes them to `SSWITCH_DROP_PORT`; this PR leaves them alone to avoid a conflict.
- **A configurable drop port**, like `--drop-port`. The primitives cannot reach the switch that runs them, so all switches of a simulation would have to share one value (the PNA NIC has a comment on the same limit).
- **The pipeline core** does not check the drop port itself: it runs the egress for a dropped packet, and it ignores a `mark_to_drop()` in its egress, because it sends the `egress_spec` of the ingress. Found while checking this PR, not fixed.

## Tasks done

Fail soft: no template → nothing asked; no filinq or no token → `unavailable` with a reason naming filinq / the key; HTTP error or an answer without a document reference → `failed` with the reason. The readable copies (`learnerName`, `validUntilLabel`, …) are written by the save after issuance, so the service derives them first through `ReadableCopiesInterface`; values the credential already carries win.

## Tasks partly done

Removing it would stop every issue, so that gate needs its own decision first.

author: pasithea0
body:
Closes #165.

## What was wrong

The home page had four rows and every one of them needed something a fresh account does not have: playback progress, recommendations (which need history), a social graph, an activity feed. `hasContent` was the OR of those, so a new local account with a catalogue behind it rendered **nothing** — and with an empty catalogue it rendered a pulsing skeleton grid that never resolved.

## Rows now

| row | needs |
|---|---|
| Continue Watching | progress |
| Recommended for You | the engine (stays first when present) |
| Friends Are Watching | a social graph |
| **What's showing** | a catalogue — trending movies + shows merged |
| **Popular on this instance** | a catalogue — minus titles the row above already showed |
| **Lists on this instance** | shared lists |
| Activity | any activity |
| Empty state | nothing at all: "Nothing here yet" + search button |

The three always-on rows are what make the page non-empty; they render from endpoints that exist today.

## Fixed on the way

- `useTrendingLists` / `usePopularLists` cast an `{items: […]}` envelope to an array, so callers iterated an object and crashed on `.map` — the home page and the community lists page both. They unwrap now.
- A trending hit's **kind comes from the endpoint**, not from its body: at `extended=min` a show carries no field a movie lacks, so guessing typed every show as a movie, collided card keys, and dropped one title from the merged row.
- The base-URL fix (`//v1/…` → host `v1`) carried by the other open PRs; without it no row loads in a browser.

## Verified (headless browser, real API)

Catalogue with three titles, no history:

```
What's showing -> Aardvark Movie, Probe Movie, Probe Show
console errors: none
```

Catalogue emptied (the five media tables truncated):

```
Nothing here yet -> (search button rendered)
```

Both screenshots taken from the running app; the populated one is attached to this PR's description in the thread.

Gates: `tsc --noEmit`, `biome check --error-on-warnings`, `pnpm test` (100).

## Not in this PR

- Recommendations still need #166 (the engine ignores the watchlist and has no provider fallback), so that row cannot appear on a fresh account yet.
- "Lists on this instance" is empty until list sharing lands (#167); it renders as soon as the endpoint returns rows.
- Upcoming/anticipated was left out: on a catalogue that has not ingested future air dates it is always empty, and an always-empty row is the thing this issue is about.

author: scrimshawlife-ctrl
body:
Next roadmap slice, for #11: "storyboard carriers beyond the digest-only index".

## Why

A storyboard's frames were linked only by the index JSON. A frame's own files said nothing about the board, a board could not be checked after the fact, and no single file carried it.

## What changed

- **Sheet.** `storyboard` also writes `storyboards/storyboard-<board_id>.svg`: one SVG that embeds every frame's `glyph.svg` byte for byte, in order, as `data:` images. Each embedded glyph keeps its own digest and root, so the board can be checked from the sheet alone.
- **`board_root`.** A commitment to the ordered frames: intent digest, sigil root and glyph bytes. It is in the index and in the sheet.
- **`storyboard-verify PATH`.** For a sheet: takes each glyph out, runs the ordinary glyph verifier on it, recomputes the board id and root, and compares them with the sheet's record. For an index: does the same from the run folders, and checks the sheet too.

## Compatibility

- The index keeps its schema name and gains `board_root`, `sheet` and per-frame `glyph_sha256`. A reader that ignores unknown keys is unaffected.
- An index written before this change still verifies, and the result says there was no root to compare.
- `construct` and single-frame output are untouched.

## Untrusted input

Sheets and indexes may come from someone else, so reading them is bounded: file size, frame count, per-frame size. An index may name run folders only by plain name (no paths, no `..`), and symlinked run folders or sheets are refused. Nothing is parsed with an XML parser.

## What it does not prove

A board proves its frames belong together and are unchanged. It does not prove who made it: anyone can build a new, self-consistent board from their own frames. The README says so.

## Checks

- Stdlib suite: 495 passed, 51 skipped. The optional-leg count is in this PR's CI.
- Tamper tests cover: reordered frames, an edited glyph, a frame from another board, a rewritten record, a removed or extra frame, a changed or missing sheet or run, path tricks in the index, symlinks, and oversized input.
- The sheet was rendered once with macOS Quick Look to confirm it displays.
- `ruff check .`, skill validator and `check` pass.

## Also in this PR

A versioning test from #41 required `Unreleased` in the changelog to be empty, which would have failed any PR that adds a changelog note. It now only requires the newest released section to match `VERSION`.

author: vitaly-sinev
body:
## What

New provider argument `advisory_lock_timeout` (milliseconds, **default `0`**) that bounds how long `pgLockRole` / `pgLockDatabase` wait for their advisory locks.

- `0` (default): unchanged, the wait is unbounded as today.
- `> 0`: `SET LOCAL lock_timeout = <n>` is applied **only around the lock acquisition**; the previous `lock_timeout` is restored right after, so the GRANT/REVOKE/ALTER statements that follow in the same transaction keep their normal lock waits. A wait over the limit returns:

  ```
  timed out after 300ms waiting for advisory lock on role "app_ro": another Terraform run or session holds it; retry, serialize the applies, or raise the provider advisory_lock_timeout (0 waits indefinitely): could not get advisory lock for role app_ro: pq: canceling statement due to lock timeout (55P03)
  ```

  Detection uses `errors.As(err, *pq.Error)` on SQLSTATE `55P03`, with a fallback on the `canceling statement due to lock timeout` message for drivers that do not expose a `*pq.Error`.

Also in the same two helpers:

- `SET statement_timeout = 0` → `SET LOCAL statement_timeout = 0` (see behavior impact).
- The member-lock query gets `ORDER BY member`, so concurrent transactions on overlapping member sets take the member locks in the same order.
- The helpers now take the `*DBConnection` every caller already has (`pgLockRole(db, txn, role)`) and read the timeout from its client config, instead of threading a new int through the call sites.

## Why

`pg_advisory_xact_lock` with `statement_timeout = 0` waits forever. When another Terraform run or a stuck session holds a role's lock, or two transactions lock overlapping member sets in opposite order, the apply just hangs with no hint of what it is waiting on. With the option enabled that becomes a fast, actionable error.

## Behavior impact

- **Default (`0`): no change.** Same statements in the same order as before, plus a deterministic `ORDER BY` on the member locks.
- `SET` → `SET LOCAL` for `statement_timeout`: within the transaction it is identical (the setting stays in effect until the transaction ends). The only difference is after `COMMIT`: a session-level `SET` survived on the connection, `SET LOCAL` does not. Today the pool keeps no idle connections (`SetMaxIdleConns(0)`), so the connection is closed when the transaction ends and the difference is not observable. Once idle connections are kept it prevents `statement_timeout = 0` leaking onto unrelated queries. (On rollback both forms were already reverted.)
- When enabled, hangs become errors. Resources of the same apply also queue on these locks (e.g. each `postgresql_database` with an `owner` holds a lock on the provider's own role while it is created), so the docs recommend a value well above how long such operations take.
- Known limitation (pre-existing design): connections are cached per DSN in `dbRegistry` together with the config of the client that opened them first. Two provider aliases pointing at the same server/user/database with different `advisory_lock_timeout` values would share the first one's value, as already happens for e.g. `superuser` / `database_username`.

## Testing

Local gate: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./postgresql/`, `gofmt -l postgresql/` (empty), `go test ./postgresql/` — all clean.

New tests (`postgresql/advisory_lock_test.go`):
- `TestIsLockTimeoutError` — `55P03` direct and wrapped, message fallback, `57014` statement timeout and unrelated errors are not matched.
- `TestProviderAdvisoryLockTimeoutDefault` — default is `0`.
- `TestAccAdvisoryLockTimeoutRoleContended` — holds the role's advisory lock from another session; `pgLockRole` with 300ms fails with the new error instead of hanging.
- `TestAccAdvisoryLockTimeoutScopedToTransaction` — on a single pooled connection with session `statement_timeout = 123s`, `lock_timeout = 45s`: inside the txn `statement_timeout` is 0 and `lock_timeout` is back to 45s after acquisition; after commit both session values are intact.
- `TestAccPostgresqlGrant_advisoryLockTimeout` — `postgresql_grant` apply with `advisory_lock_timeout = 300` fails with the new error while the lock is held; with the default the same grant applies once the lock is released.

The acceptance tests were checked against mutations: session-level `SET`, dropping the `lock_timeout` restore, and disabling the `55P03` detection each make the corresponding test fail.

Full acceptance suite on PostgreSQL 16 (stock `postgres:16`, `wal_level=logical`):

| Profile | Result | Baseline `main` |
|---|---|---|
| superuser | **100 PASS / 3 SKIP / 2 FAIL** | 95 / 3 / 2 |
| rds (non-superuser, `tests/switch_rds.sh`) | **68 PASS / 37 SKIP / 0 FAIL** | 63 / 37 / 0 |

The +5 are the new tests. The 2 superuser failures are `TestAccPostgresqlSecurityLabel_Basic/_Update` (`dummy` label provider not loaded in the stock image), same as baseline. In the superuser run three grant tests (`TestAccPostgresqlGrant`, `GrantColumns`, `GrantObjects`) first hit `dial tcp ...: can't assign requested address` (local ephemeral port exhaustion while other suites were running on the same host) and passed on rerun.

Closes #10

author: freeesta
body:
## Cosa cambia
UNTARGET-WP3 PR 1. The per-stage diagnosis (`tools/area_synthetic.py` + `tools/area_diagnosis.py`) shows that the feature-table area differs from the XIC area for two reasons. The first is **channel binning**, already fixed opt-in by `area_from=window`. The second is the **integration rule**: Σy × the *median* MS1 interval, where MZmine and the chromatogram use a trapezoid on the real RT. That rule is still wrong in `window` mode whenever MS1 spacing is uneven (DDA: MS2 scans at the apex).

This PR adds a third value, `area_from=xic`. The row area becomes the trapezoid of the ±6 ppm quality trace on the real retention times (`quality::trapezoid`). It applies to every algorithm and to the pieces of `resolve`. Gap-filled cells use the same rule (`FillParams::xic`). **No default changes**: `channel` and `strict` stay the defaults, and the new fields appear in the `Debug` fingerprints only when on.

Signed log2 median / p95 of |log2|, 60 synthetic peaks per scenario (jitter = m/z noise scan to scan; DDA = top-5 MS2 when an ion ≥ 1e6). "vs XIC" = row area / trapezoid of the ±10 ppm XIC over the row's scans:

| scenario | channel (default) vs XIC | window vs XIC | **xic** vs XIC | channel vs true | **xic** vs true | xic+wide vs true |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| clean | +0.001 / 0.004 | +0.001 / 0.004 | **−0.000 / 0.000** | −0.001 / 0.019 | −0.003 / 0.021 | −0.003 / 0.021 |
| ±1 ppm | −0.058 / 0.151 | +0.003 / 0.022 | **−0.000 / 0.000** | −0.089 / 0.573 | −0.006 / 0.473 | −0.004 / 0.022 |
| ±2 ppm | −0.154 / 0.372 | +0.035 / 0.104 | **+0.000 / 0.003** | −0.898 / 2.237 | −0.667 / 1.963 | −0.131 / 1.046 |
| ±3 ppm | −0.112 / 0.435 | +0.061 / 0.212 | **−0.000 / 0.223** | −1.915 / 2.960 | −1.802 / 3.023 | −1.298 / 2.181 |
| drift 4 ppm | −0.053 / 0.177 | +0.002 / 0.024 | **−0.000 / 0.000** | −0.096 / 0.841 | −0.009 / 0.739 | −0.006 / 0.200 |
| DDA | −0.545 / 0.760 | −0.478 / 0.665 | **−0.000 / 0.000** | −0.584 / 0.935 | −0.008 / 0.504 | −0.004 / 0.044 |

The residual gap vs XIC with window+wide comes **only from the rule stage**: +0.005 (±2 ppm), +0.037 (±3 ppm), −0.482 (DDA). With `xic` it is 0.000 in every scenario, and 0.000 with `xic`+`wide` too (p95 ≤ 0.014, except ±3 ppm: 0.15–0.22, from points outside the ±6 ppm window). The remaining gap vs the *true* area is splitting by `stitch=strict` (11/60 peaks split at ±1 ppm, 50/60 at ±2 ppm). That is a scientific default for Federico, so it is not touched here.

Tests: `flow_area_tests.rs` checks uneven MS1 scans: window is 1.1 log2 off the XIC, xic is 0.0000. A `--set det.area_from=xic` run reaches the plan and the meta. `gapfill` gets a unit test of the trapezoid and of the fingerprint. The methods sentence comes from `AREA_XIC`. The parity test `test_the_xic_area_gives_the_same_bytes_native_and_in_node` (native = wasm bytes) is in `tests/test_feat_wasm.py`. It is skipped locally (no `wasm-bindgen` here) and runs in CI. Generated files were regenerated with their tools: `steps-1.json`, `strumenti-*.json`, and the two `tests/data/assist/reg/*.jsonl` recordings, because the step catalog text changed (`MZLAB_UPDATE_LLM=1`).

Raw wasm sizes are recorded in `docs/agenti/wasm-tetti-misure.md`: `hr` 3 830 826 → 3 831 434 B (+0.016 %), `untargeted` −181 B, `rotte` unchanged.

Closes #305

## 概要

手元の clone の `origin` を、リポジトリの今の名前 `git@github.com:tumeda1992/nanitabe.git` に変えた。この変更は手元の設定であり、この PR には含まれない。
`.agents/skills/tumeda-dev-plugin-context.md` の `origin` の記述を、変えた後の事実に合わせた。

## 背景

旧名 `setsumaru1992/nanitabe` の URL は GitHub が転送するため、`origin` が旧名のままでも push できる。
そのため `git remote -v` を見ると、旧名を今の名前と取り違える。#297 の作業ではこれが起きた。

「`git remote -v` の値だけを見て判断しない」という注意は既に書いてあった。ただし push や PR の手順を考える時にしか読まれない節にあり、リポジトリ名を他の用途で使う場面には届かなかった。
注意書きを増やすのではなく、`origin` を今の名前にして、取り違えの元をなくした。

- `git remote -v` が `tumeda1992/nanitabe` を指し、fetch でき、`origin/main` が #304 の merge（`fa861a9`）と一致する。

author: clintg6
body:
## Summary

Compute row and head offsets in `_fused_qk_rope_cat_and_cache_mla_kernel` in 64 bits. This fixes a GPU memory access fault on long prefill chunks.

In SGLang, this fault stops the server for DSA models (GLM-5.x, DeepSeek-V3.2) when one prefill chunk is long enough. For example, GLM-5.x at TP2 with `--chunked-prefill-size 131072`, as in the GLM-5.3 recipes, crashes on any prompt longer than 116,508 tokens. The limit depends on query heads per rank (see the table below), so DeepSeek-V3.2 hits the same limit at TP4. With this fix, those prompts prefill in one chunk.

## Motivation

The kernel derives `pid_b` and `pid_hq` from `tl.program_id(0)`, so `pid_b * stride_b` and `pid_hq * stride_h` are computed in int32. With `QH` query heads per rank and `B` tokens in one launch of an MLA layer (512 + 64 dims), these products overflow when either:

- `B x QH x 576 > 2^31 - 1` (`q_out` row stride), or
- `(QH - 1) x B x 512 > 2^31 - 1` (SGLang passes `q_nope` as a transposed BMM output, so its head stride is `B x 512`).

When that happens the kernel reads and writes outside its tensors and the server dies with a memory fault.

SGLang calls this kernel on gfx950 in DSA prefill (GLM-5.x, DeepSeek-V3.2 with the `tilelang`/`triton` DSA backend), where `B` can be as large as `--chunked-prefill-size`:

| Query heads per rank | Example | Faults above |
|---|---|---|
| 64 | GLM-5.x TP1, DeepSeek-V3.2 TP2 | 58,254 tokens |
| 32 | GLM-5.x TP2, DeepSeek-V3.2 TP4 | 116,508 tokens |
| 16 | GLM-5.x TP4, DeepSeek-V3.2 TP8 | 233,016 tokens |
| 8 | GLM-5.x TP8 | 466,033 tokens |

We found it on GLM-5.3-MXFP4, MI355X TP2, `--chunked-prefill-size 131072`, with a single 130,207-token prompt:

```
Memory Fault Error [..., kernel: _fused_qk_rope_cat_and_cache_mla_kernel_QH_32_KH_1_...]
```

## Changes

- `aiter/ops/triton/_triton_kernels/fusions/fused_kv_cache.py`: cast `pid_hq` and `pid_b` to `tl.int64`. Every row and head offset is then computed in 64 bits. The KV-cache write already indexes by an int64 slot, and the column offsets were already int64.

```diff
-        pid_hq = pid // B
-        pid_b = pid % B
+        pid_hq = (pid // B).to(tl.int64)
+        pid_b = (pid % B).to(tl.int64)
```

- `op_tests/triton_tests/fusions/test_fused_kv_cache.py`: add `test_fused_qk_rope_cat_and_cache_mla_int64_offsets`, a regression test for offsets past `2^31 - 1`.

No API change. Outputs are unchanged for sizes that did not overflow before.

## Testing

- [x] Unit tests added or updated
- [ ] Performance benchmarks run
- [ ] Tested on MI250X
- [ ] Tested on MI300X

Tested on MI355X (gfx950) only; details below.

## Documentation

- [x] No documentation change is needed, with the reason stated below

This is an internal kernel fix with no change to the interface or behavior at valid sizes.

## Dependencies

- [x] No new third-party dependencies added

## Breaking Changes

None.

## PR Self-Review

### Reviewed revision

`ac81177`

### Behavior and intent

Only the index math changes, from int32 to int64, for the token row (`pid_b`) and query head (`pid_hq`). Before this change, any launch where `B x QH x 576` or `(QH - 1) x B x 512` exceeds `2^31 - 1` computed wrapped addresses and faulted (or silently corrupted memory). After it, these launches address correctly. Smaller launches give bit-identical results.

### Validation and unverified scope

Hardware: MI355X. Shapes: GLM-5.3 TP2 (32 query heads, FP8 KV cache, FP8 `q_out`, interleaved RoPE, SGLang's transposed `q_nope`). Script: standalone repro (not added to `op_tests/`).

```
python test_rope_cache_overflow.py save  16384 ref.pt     # unpatched
python test_rope_cache_overflow.py check 16384 ref.pt     # patched
python test_rope_cache_overflow.py chunk 131072 16384     # patched
python test_rope_cache_overflow.py chunk 262144 16384     # patched
```

| Check | Tokens | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Patched vs unpatched | 16,384 | `q_out`, `k_pe_out`, KV cache bit-identical |
| Patched, one launch vs 16K-token launches | 131,072 | bit-identical |
| Patched, one launch vs 16K-token launches | 262,144 | bit-identical |

New op test (MI355X):

```
pytest op_tests/triton_tests/fusions/test_fused_kv_cache.py -k int64_offsets
```

| Kernel | Result |
|---|---|
| This PR | passed (3.6 s) |
| `pid_hq` cast removed | failed: `q_out` mismatch (9.7% of elements) |
| `pid_b` cast removed | memory access fault (process aborted) |
| Both casts removed (`main`) | memory access fault (process aborted) |

The existing `test_fused_qk_rope_cat_and_cache_mla` cases still pass.

End to end: with this fix (plus a matching SGLang sparse-MLA int64 fix), GLM-5.3-MXFP4 TP2 servers prefill ~131K-token prompts in one 131,072-token chunk with no fault. RULER2 128K scored 100% across 56 prompts.

Not verified:
- MI250X and MI300X: not run.
- Performance impact of the int64 index math: not benchmarked. I expect it to be negligible, since it adds two casts per program in a memory-bound kernel.
- NeoX RoPE, the NoPE path, shuffled KV cache, and non-FP8 dtypes: not run at overflow sizes. They share the same offset code.
- DeepSeek-V3.2: the rows in the table above come from the formula, not from runs.
- The `aiter` MLA backend's absorb path (decode and short extends): `B` stays small there, so it does not reach the overflow.

### PR-specific question

> What is the most important boundary or failure mode introduced by this change, and what evidence covers it?

The boundary is the int32 limit on the row and head offsets, `pid_b * stride_b` and `pid_hq * stride_h`. They overflow when `B x QH x 576 > 2^31 - 1` (`q_out`) or `(QH - 1) x B x 512 > 2^31 - 1` (transposed `q_nope`). For 32 heads, that is above 116,508 tokens. Evidence:
- Below the boundary nothing changes: at 16,384 tokens the patched and unpatched kernels give bit-identical `q_out`, `k_pe_out` and KV cache.
- The new op test crosses the boundary for both offsets in one launch (36,864 tokens, 128 heads). It fails if either cast is removed.
- Above the boundary the result is correct: at 131,072 and 262,144 tokens, one launch is bit-identical to the same work split into 16K-token launches, where no launch overflows.
- End to end: before the fix, a 130,207-token prompt faulted in this kernel. After it, the same prompt prefills in one chunk.

The change itself could only break things if the int64 math changed results or cost speed. Results are bit-identical. Speed was not benchmarked; the change adds two casts per program in a memory-bound kernel.

### Changed op tests

`op_tests/triton_tests/fusions/test_fused_kv_cache.py`: adds `test_fused_qk_rope_cat_and_cache_mla_int64_offsets`.

- **What it covers:** one launch with 36,864 tokens and 128 query heads, using FP8 `q_out`, an FP8 KV cache and a transposed `q_nope`, as SGLang calls the kernel. In this launch, `q_out` row offsets reach 2.7e9 and `q_nope` head offsets reach 2.4e9, both past `2^31 - 1`. It compares `q_out`, `k_pe_out` and the KV cache bit for bit with the same work run in 4,096-token launches, where `q_nope` is made contiguous so no offset passes `2^31 - 1`.
- **Why it isn't redundant:** the existing MLA tests stop at 2,048 tokens and 16 heads, far below the boundary, so they pass with or without this fix.
- **Cost:** about 11 GB of device memory and 4 s on MI355X. It skips on GPUs with less than 32 GiB and on gfx1250, which runs the gluon kernel.

author: yadgarhq-bot[bot]
body:
## What

Moves the `yadgarhq/actions` hook block of `yadgarhq/chart` from `v1.65.4` to `v1.65.5`. The block is regenerated from the `chart` class (topic `yadgar-class-chart`), as `classes.json` in `yadgarhq/actions` defines it.

The hook ids, their order and their keys already match the class, so the `rev:` line is the only change.

No other block of `.pre-commit-config.yaml` changed.

## Why

ADR-0982: an `actions` release opens one adoption pull request per consumer, found by its class topic. ADR-0561 rules that a release fires them; ADR-0635 rules that a hook set is generated from its class. Before this, every rev bump was a hand edit and nothing detected drift.

Opened by the `fan-out` workflow in `yadgarhq/actions`, as the `yadgarhq-bot` App. It proposes and never merges (ADR-0690, ADR-0531). ADR-0983: the run's report says which consumers carry `v1.65.5`.

## Changelog

No release: a hook adoption changes developer tooling only, so this body carries no Conventional Commits entry and the `version` job cuts no tag for it.

## Verification

`ci / passed` on this pull request runs this repository's pre-commit at the new rev; that run IS the verification. Nothing was run before the pull request was opened. A repository with no CI needs `pre-commit run --all-files` on this branch before the merge.

The release range to read: https://github.com/yadgarhq/actions/compare/v1.65.4...v1.65.5

## Risk

Merging cuts no release of this repository. The hook block is developer tooling and is not part of what the repository ships, so the change waits for the next release a person cuts.

A newer hook can red a check that passed at the old rev. That is the gate working: fix the cause in its own pull request, and never widen the gate to make it pass.

A commit a person adds to this branch lands with no release, because the squash keeps the bot as author. Put such a fix in its own pull request.

Reversible: restore `rev: v1.65.4`. A published tag never moves, so the old rev still names the same hooks.

D80: this changes developer tooling only. It renders no resource, names no cloud and no ingress implementation, and adds no trust boundary.

author: macbet
body:
Terrakube never sends JSON:API `links`; it pages through `meta.page`. The old code followed `links.next`, so `List` always stopped after one response and results were silently capped at the server limit (500 or 10,000 depending on the type).

**What changed**

- `List` with no page options requests `page[totals]` and fetches every page for the seven resource types the server can page: workspace, workspace tag, action, federated, agent, organization variable, workspace access. All other types send exactly the request they sent before.
- If the server answers the first paged request with 400, the list is fetched once without page parameters: which types a server pages can differ by version and caller.
- Links in responses are no longer followed. This also removes the unbounded next-link loop and the token being sent to whatever host a link named.
- `Page` / `PageSize` on a resource type the server cannot paginate now return a `*ValidationError` without sending a request, instead of a server 400. This is a behavior change for callers that set them on those types.
- `doList` is the only list decoder; `doListWithLinks` and `fetchAllPages` are gone.

**Verified against Terrakube 2.34.1**

- Default listing of workspaces in 7 organizations equals a manual `Page`/`PageSize: 10` walk.
- With the page size forced to 10 through a transport, a collection of 38 workspaces is fetched in 4 requests: 38 records, no duplicates, same order as one unpaged request; a filter is sent on every page.
- Unpaged types (jobs, modules) still send one request with no page parameters.

Not verified live: the 400 fallback (unit test only), and the nine types that had no data on the server (they are treated as unpaged). Row order across pages without `sort` is tracked in #50.

Closes #33, closes #34, closes #35, closes #36

author: mtdowling
body:
## Summary

Three bugs found by live check 2, in a second Kiro Crew gateway (`KIROCREW_HOME` set to a temp folder) on Linux. Fakes never showed them.

- **A second Kiro Crew home shared the main crew's Avoozl catalog.** Kiro Crew passes `KIROCREW_HOME` to an app's backend and MCP server but not `XDG_*`, so a test gateway's Avoozl opened `~/.config/avoozl` and `~/.local/state/avoozl/catalog.sqlite`, the main crew's files. Now a `KIROCREW_HOME` other than `~/.kiro/crew` keeps Avoozl's config and state in `<KIROCREW_HOME>/avoozl/`. The main home, named or not, keeps the old places. Symlinked homes compare by real path.
- **A fresh install's tick paused itself for good.** Before any workspace exists, every `avoozl-tick` run failed with "no workspace". Kiro Crew pauses a cron after 5 errors in a row, and it stayed paused after the person added a workspace. The cron's own tick call now answers `{skipped: true}` and the cron raises Skip. Other callers still get the error.
- **A chat folder with no project directory still waited with no notice** (finding 1 of the first live check). The cron now reads its folders and sends `folders` to `plans_tick`. A dispatch whose folder has no project directory waits, and one `decision` notice names the folder and the checkout path to set. Same notice each tick, queued once.

## Tested

- `npm test`: 950 pass, 0 fail (Linux)
- New tests: "a second Kiro Crew home gets its own Avoozl config and catalog", "the cron's tick with no workspace is a skip, not an error", "a ready leaf whose chat folder has no project directory waits with one notice"; the tick.py harness tests now expect the folder read
- Live, in the isolated gateway: catalog at `<KIROCREW_HOME>/avoozl/state/catalog.sqlite`; the tick ran with a workspace; the folder notice reached Kiro Crew's notification log with the checkout path
- `format:check`, `git diff --check`, release scan: clean (no local terms file on this machine)

author: cb1kenobi
body:
Fixes SIG-426. Two Windows-only flakes in `packages/cli/test/new-tui.test.ts`, both of which passed on rerun:

1. `Hook timed out in 10000ms` at `afterAll(removeTempDirs)` in `test/setup.ts`, after every test had passed (PR #419, node 24 / windows-latest).
2. A scaffolded app's own `describes itself` test timed out at 5000 ms (run 42989858742, node 24 / windows-latest). The child's own summary in that log says `Duration 11.06s (transform 64%, ...)`.

## The cleanup hook

- **Each app is removed when its test ends.** `materialize()` registers `removeTempDir(app)` in the test's own `onTestFinished`. Counted at the `afterAll` on macOS, the sixteen apps were 1,719 of about 3,400 entries the hook had to remove, so it now has about half as much to do. A per-test removal is not `afterEach`, which belongs to the file and would reach other tests' directories.
- **A test that times out reaps its children before its app is removed** (review round 1). See "Reaping a timed-out test's children" below.
- **`removeTempDirs()` is asynchronous and concurrent.** `rmSync` removed each directory in turn, so each directory's retry waits added up, and vitest counts a slow synchronous hook too. The directories are now removed together with `Promise.allSettled`. A directory that cannot be removed still fails the file.
- **The hook has a budget of 60 seconds** (`REMOVAL_TIMEOUT`, used in each package's `setup.ts`). The budget only limits a hang: a directory that cannot be removed does not hang, because `rm` stops retrying and throws. The four `temp.ts` copies are still byte-identical.

Locally (macOS), the hook went from 162 ms to 58 ms and `new-tui.test.ts` from 31.5 s to 31.3 s.

## The scaffolded app's own test: no new timeout in the scaffold

The 5 seconds were spent by the harness, not the app. `link()` makes `@ttylabs/sigil` a junction to the workspace. Vite follows the junction to `packages/sigil/dist`, which has no `node_modules` in its path, so vitest transforms every runtime module itself. An installed app hands them to node. I measured the same single/JSX/JS app both ways, with a `registerHooks()` probe on node's loader:

| `@ttylabs/sigil` is | runtime modules node loaded | `describes itself` | run |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a junction to the workspace (the harness) | 0 | 72 ms | 234 ms, transform 51% |
| a copy under `node_modules` (an install) | 73 | 14 ms | 116 ms |

So the scaffold keeps vitest's 5-second default. A real app does not need more, and every new app would carry the number. The harness's own `vitest run` passes `--testTimeout=30000`. That is six times the default and well inside the 180 s the variant test gives the whole app.

### A defect this found, not fixed here

Linking the copy would be the faithful fix, but it fails the two JSX apps whose component is behind a command. With the runtime handed to node, `runCommand()` loads `src/commands/ops.*` with node's own `import()`, and that `import()` cannot load the component: `Unknown file extension ".tsx"` (and `.jsx` for JS). The app's own `refuses without a terminal` therefore fails in an installed app, made with `sigil new --tui-command ops --syntax jsx`. The harness passes it only because vite handled that `import()`. I recorded it as a known defect under `sigil new` in `packages/cli/AGENTS.md`. It needs a ticket of its own.

## Reaping a timed-out test's children (review round 1)

The first version passed the test's `signal` to `spawn()`. Review found two problems with that, and both were real:

- **`spawn()`'s own `signal` rejects at the abort, with the child still alive.** When a test times out, vitest aborts the signal and runs `onTestFinished` straight away, so the removal raced the child's exit.
- **Killing the child does not kill what it started.** I measured this on macOS with `ps`: SIGTERM or SIGKILL of a nested `vitest run` left its `forks.js` worker running under pid 1. My round-1 claim that "no child process was still running" was wrong. The `pgrep` pattern I used did not match `forks.js`.

What the code does now:

- **`spawnNode()` settles only on `close`, aborts included.** On abort it ends the whole process tree:
  - **POSIX (since review round 2):** `endTree()` reads the tree from `ps -A -o pid=,ppid=` and walks it down from the child. Each process it finds gets SIGSTOP before the next look, so nothing can start another process in between. Once a look finds nothing new, every one of them gets SIGKILL. Since review round 3, that SIGKILL is in a `finally`, so a look that fails still kills everything already stopped. `ps` runs with a 5-second timeout. A look that fails (a spawn error, a non-zero exit, a signal, or an empty listing) throws an error naming `ps`. The child's promise rejects with that error, and the hook fails the test with it once the directory is removed. The review round 1 fix spawned the child `detached` and killed its group instead. The next section explains why that was dropped.
  - **Windows:** `taskkill /pid <pid> /T /F`, which walks the tree by parent pid. Windows has no process groups, and killing a process there kills only that one process.
- **`materialize()` keeps every child's promise, and its `onTestFinished` waits for all of them before `removeTempDir()`.** A child that never closes holds the hook until `REMOVAL_TIMEOUT` (60 s). That fails the test and leaves the directory to the file's `afterAll`.
- **`removeTempDir()` remembers what it removed, and `removeTempDirs()` checks those directories again when the file ends.** Any that exist again are removed a second time and fail the file with `<dir> was written to after it was removed`.

Sabotage on macOS, with all twelve variants timing out:

| code | timeout | directories left | `forks.js` workers left |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| review round 2 (`endTree()`) | 250, 350, 450, 550 ms | 0 | 0 |
| review round 1 (`detached`, group kill) | 250, 350, 450, 550 ms | 0 | 0 |
| round 1 (signal to `spawn()`) | 350 ms | 0 | 1 |
| round 1 (signal to `spawn()`) | 400 ms | 0 | 1 |

For `endTree()` I logged which child each abort ended. At 250 ms, 8 of the 12 were nested vitests and 4 were the app itself. From 350 ms up, every one was a nested vitest.

To prove the re-check, I removed the reaping (no tree kill, and no waiting for children before removal) and ran the whole `new-tui.test.ts`. The `afterAll` failed with four apps `written to after it was removed`, and nothing was left behind. The re-check only sees a write that lands before the file ends. A later write is what `pnpm test:leaks` is for.

In the case of failure 2, a test timed out *inside* the child vitest. That child had exited before the parent went on: `node()` waits for `close`, and vitest's `ForksPoolWorker.stop()` waits for each fork to exit before vitest itself exits. So that case never left a worker behind.

## When `ps` fails (review round 3)

Before this fix, `endTree()` read `spawnSync('ps').stdout` without checking it and with no timeout:

- **`ps` failed to spawn:** `.trim()` threw between the SIGSTOPs and the SIGKILLs, so the stopped processes were never killed and never closed.
- **`ps` exited non-zero with no output:** the walk found no descendants, so it killed only the root.

Verification:

- **New test `ending a process tree`** (POSIX only). It starts a real root and child, then makes the first look fail (a missing command, ENOENT) or the second (`false`, exit 1). It checks that `endTree()` throws naming `ps`, that the root died of SIGKILL, and, when the second look fails, that the child died too.
- **Sabotage of the test.** Without the `finally`, both cases fail with `expected 'still there' to be 'SIGKILL'`. Waiting for the root is raced against 5 s, so a root left stopped fails the test and still reaches the test's own cleanup. Without the checks, both fail with `expected [Function] to throw an error`.
- **End to end.** With the default command switched to `false` and all twelve variants timing out at 400 ms, each test's hook failed

author: guisatierf
body:
## What

Adds a **Problemas** page to the team menu (admins only) that lists the errors the web app and the worker logged, so the team sees a failing flow before a customer reports it.

- **Recording.** A second listener next to the existing error alerts keeps error-level logs, plus publications that failed for good and failed stock syncs, in a new `problem_events` table. Entries are buffered in memory, grouped by a fingerprint (same process, event and message, with ids and numbers ignored) and written every 2 seconds. Repeats of an open problem within a day add to its counter. Writing never throws or holds the request or job; a failed write is reported on stderr at most once a minute. Values that look like tokens, e-mails or CPF/CNPJ are removed before storage, on top of the logger's own key-based redaction. Problems unseen for 30 days are pruned, with a 5,000-row cap.
- **Page.** `/admin/problemas` lists problems newest first, filtered by open/resolved, period (24 hours, 7 days, 30 days) and area (publishing, sync, orders, payments, invoices, e-mail, other), with cursor pagination. Each row shows the message, area, when, how many times, and the account and store when known, linked to the admin customer page. The detail page shows the stored context and has "Marcar como resolvido" with undo on the notice.
- **Access.** The page and every server function check the existing `audit.view` permission (admins only) on the server.

## Database

Adds the `problem_events` table and the `problem_area` and `problem_service` enums (migration `0071_problem_events`). No changes to existing tables. No new environment variables or dependencies.

## Notes for review

- Sidebar: the only change under navigation is one `ADMIN_NAV_ITEMS` entry and its icon mapping in `action-icons.ts`.
- The logger now supports several warning/error listeners instead of one; the existing webhook alerts keep listening to errors only.

## Tests

- Unit: capture (area, fingerprint, redaction of a token, e-mail and CPF in fields and messages, size caps), repository (dedupe window, reopen after resolve, pagination, account lookup, retention and row cap, undo), recorder (counts repeats, stores no personal data, survives a database outage), access and cursor.
- E2E: an admin finds a seeded problem, resolves it, undoes, resolves again; an agent and a reseller cannot open the page (passing locally). `/admin/problemas` was added to the accessibility sweep. The full Playwright suite is being run locally on this commit; the result will be added as a comment.
- The screenshot board (desktop and 375 px, light and dark) was approved in chat.

## Origin

Requested by Guilherme on 12–13/11/2026 in the SellBridge chat: "Tem algum lugar pra mostrar os erros no admin com umas logs e afins?", then "Eu quis dizer no próprio painel de admin para algum dev ir lá e ver se deu algum problema".

author: 0x1ocean
body:
Track 1 (story 1, one Banda on every machine), slice SE5, PR 1, the engine's part. Serves principle 9 of `docs/what-we-build.md` and ADR 0124.

## Why

SE5 opens the same window in any browser at a machine's door. The door answered a plain `GET /` with one line, and nothing served the page outside Banda's app.

## What

- **A browser gets the page, `curl` the line.** `GET /` with `Accept: text/html` answers the page Banda's app shows; anything else still gets "Banda on arc · <host key>".
- **Where the files are.** The page's build: `web/dist` beside the engine's program, where a packed app already has it for its own window, or `client/web/dist` in a checkout. `BANDA_PAGE_FILES` names another folder. An engine with no page answers as before.
- **What the page may load.** Each answer carries a policy: its own files and its own door, no script written into it, nothing that frames it.
- **Only that folder.** A file is read by a path of plain names, and a link that leads out of the folder is no file of the page.
- **Behind the door's own roads.** The WebSocket and a file's bytes answer for themselves. The API's port serves no page.

The page alone is nobody: what it does, it does as a paired device on the door's WebSocket. Nothing the Person sees in Banda's app changes.

## Not in this PR

- The engine's own copy and its tarball do not carry the page yet (next PR, which touches `scripts/engine.mjs`).
- Without the desktop the page still says it needs Banda's app, until the browser's adapter and its pairing screen (SE5, PR 2, after the mocks).
- The files go whole and uncompressed: #1700.

## Checked

`scripts/check.sh --no-window`. Unit tests of the page's router (the two answers of `/`, the policy, a file, six paths that leave the folder, a link out of it) and one against a running engine (the page, a file, `curl`'s line, `/ws` and `/b/` still their own, no page on the API's port). One review round; nothing it had to fix, four things it suggested are in.

author: unarbos
body: ## What this changes Jacob's go-live rule: no burn, in any case. No weight goes to UID 0 or to the owner as a fallback. A follow-up to #102, in `v2/sn120_v2/weights_writer.py` and its test file only. - The writer never submits a table with weight on `burn_uid` (UID 0). - The registered kings of the window split all the weight. This holds with fewer than 10 kings and when a king is deregistered. - When no king of the window is registered, or when there is no king yet, the writer submits nothing. The receipt is `deferred`, and the last valid weights stay on chain. - The dry run prints `"status": "would defer"` with that reason in the same case. ## The old rule `payout.weights` returns `{burn_uid: 1.0}` when no payee is paid. That came from the v2 spec, in the payout line: "Unearned weight burns to UID 0. Nonzero floor." The writer used to submit that table when the chain snapshot was complete and the state had loaded. This change does not touch `v2/sn120_v2/payout.py`, which the foundation owns. The writer refuses that table, and it also holds if `payout.weights` later returns an empty table or raises. ## Tests `cd v2 && python -m pytest`: 545 passed, 1 skipped. - `test_fewer_kings_than_the_window_split_all_the_weight_and_uid_0_gets_none` - `test_an_outage_keeps_the_last_valid_weights_and_defers`, with the new case "no king is registered" - `test_a_first_run_with_an_outage_or_with_no_registered_king_submits_nothing`, with the new cases "no king yet" and "no king is registered" One manual read-only check against finney: `--dry-run` on a journal of the CPU simulation, where no king is on chain, printed `would defer` and wrote nothing.

author: ecto
body:
Two sidebar fixes: the timestamp that competed with the git badge, and the badge that vanished under the pointer.

## The badge that pops out on hover

`Sidebar.swift` gated the row's `GitBadgeView` on `!expandTitle` — and hover for 450 ms sets `expandTitle`, so the badge was **removed from the layout** under the cursor. The old comment called it deliberate ("the meta steps aside for the title"); it read as a bug because the badge blinks out, which teaches you it's unreliable.

**Fix:** drop the gate. The badge stays for as long as the pointer is on the row; the title may truncate a little sooner, which is the honest trade — the badge is information, truncation is not.

**Red proof (run, not claimed):** the test uses a `SidebarProbe` that counts how often the badge enters the layout, and asserts it appears *more* after `expandTitle` fires than before. Reintroducing the old gate (`if let git, !expandTitle`) fails it:

```
** TEST FAILED **  (testBadgeStaysInTheRowWhileHovered)
```

— the probe sees the badge leave the row exactly when the title expands.

## The timestamp

Removed from the two-line row: `14m`/`26m`/`1h` competed with the git badge for the same slot. Also removed the dead branch around it — the `if live == .running` and its `else` rendered **identical** `Text`s, so the condition did nothing.

**`SessionAgeShort` callers left alone:** the compact strip and the archive view keep their ages (there the age *is* the useful signal); the iOS app doesn't render it. The sort stays activity-based; the order is no longer labelled on the two-line row, but the compact strip still shows ages, so nothing is unexplained everywhere.

## Verified

- `SidebarHoverBadgeTests`: 4/4 — the red proof above, plus rest/hover-300ms/hover-600ms frames where the badge is present and the row width is unchanged across all three.
- Snapshots for the same three states, light and dark.
- Web sidebar: **neither issue exists there** — no age column on the row and no hover-hidden badge — so nothing to keep in sync.

The stale-suite run in this branch's history (exit 65, 3 failures) was the pre-#325 decode pair plus a benchmark 0.1 ms over budget under load; both predate this branch and #325's fix has since landed on main.

author: rudrankriyam
body:
## What was wrong

The Game Center v2, leaderboard relationship, leaderboard set member localization and achievement relationship client methods each repeated the same request code by hand: an option loop, next-URL validation, the query string, `c.do`, `json.Unmarshal` and the error wrapping. #3553 added shared request helpers (`getJSON`, `sendJSON`, `sendNoContent`, `applyOptions`) for this.

## What changed (+209/−913, 1 commit)

67 methods now call the helpers. The path expressions, query builders, payload literals, pre-checks, their order and the error prefixes are copied verbatim.

| File | Methods | Converted | Left hand-written |
|---|---|---|---|
| `client_game_center_v2.go` | 52 | 48 | 4 delegating |
| `client_game_center_leaderboards_relationships.go` | 6 | 6 | 0 |
| `client_game_center_leaderboard_set_member_localizations.go` | 7 | 6 | 1 delegating |
| `client_game_center_leaderboards_relationships_v2.go` | 4 | 4 | 0 |
| `client_game_center_achievements_relationships.go` | 3 | 3 | 0 |

By shape: 11 list GETs (`applyOptions` + `getJSON`), 15 single GETs (`getJSON`), 19 POST/PATCH with a decoded response (`sendJSON`), 14 relationship POST/PATCH/DELETE with a body (`sendNoContent(..., payload)`), 8 DELETEs (`sendNoContent(..., nil)`).

These stay hand-written because they only call other client methods and send no request of their own: `UploadGameCenterAchievementImageV2`, `UploadGameCenterLeaderboardImageV2`, `UploadGameCenterLeaderboardSetImageV2`, `SetGameCenterLeaderboardSetMembersV2` and `GetGameCenterLeaderboardSetMemberLocalization`.

`client_request.go` is unchanged.

## Why this approach

This applies the helpers merged in #3553, following the same per-file conversion used for the devices, actors and retention message clients. The 11 query builders that `getJSON` now also evaluates when a next URL is given only fill a `url.Values`, so evaluating them on later pages changes nothing.

## Evidence

All results below are on head `012f4bddd`, merge base `f20593e95`.

- **Request shape per method:** `diff <(clienttuples <merge-base tree>) <(clienttuples <worktree>)` prints nothing. The tool records each method's checks, HTTP method, path, query, body, next-URL handling, decoding and error wrapping. Every converted method is still classified REQ; the per-file counts did not change.
- **Test list:** `go test ./internal/asc/ -list '.*'` is identical before and after (1,827 tests).
- **No test changes:** `git diff --name-only f20593e95 HEAD | grep _test.go` prints nothing.
- **Package tests:** `ASC_BYPASS_KEYCHAIN=1 go test ./internal/asc/ -count=1` passes.
- **Full gate:** `make build`, `make format`, `make check-docs`, `make lint` and `ASC_BYPASS_KEYCHAIN=1 make test` all PASS.
- **CLI surface:** `0 differences across 1997 command paths and 3987 validation probes`.
- **Full-branch review:** no actionable findings (review head `012f4bddd`, base `f20593e95`).
- **Request comparison:** run against a local fake API with `--filter "game-center"`, the only command family that calls these methods (`internal/cli/gamecenter`). Result: `0 differences across 953 invocations (688 made at least one request)`, 218 leaf commands, 233 distinct API paths. The paths include the v2 achievement, leaderboard and leaderboard set endpoints, `/v1/gameCenterLeaderboardSetMemberLocalizations` and `/v1/gameCenterLeaderboardSets/{id}/relationships/gameCenterLeaderboards`.

The nine relationship `Update*` methods in the relationship files have no CLI caller. Their request shape is covered by their existing HTTP tests in `client_http_issue_617_*` and `client_http_issue_618_*`, which pass unchanged, and by the empty tuple diff.

## Tests

No tests were added, removed or changed.

## Compatibility

No user-visible change. Commands, flags, help, output, exit codes, error text and HTTP requests are identical.

author: travis-mcdevitt
body:
Tetris never launched because Goblin Link put a generic script into PortMaster's Ports folder, where the installed PortMaster launcher requires its own metadata. Apps and games now share standalone NextUI Tools Paks. The wrapper starts in the installed entry point directory, records the exit status, and caps stdout/stderr at 64 KiB per launch. Existing owned Ports entries are removed when replaced; unrelated entries are preserved, and app/game title collisions are rejected.

`build.logs` exposes only the active profile's installed app/game diagnostics under existing build consent, without executing anything or widening shell/file access. Build instructions now require verified/bundled dependencies, relative paths, device controls, and owner launch verification. NextUI's optional Python/pygame/PortMaster are no longer assumed. Docs include a native launcher template.

Closes #29.

Owner approval: “Great make the changes that give that a greater chance of success, then reprompt muse on my phone to make the fixes”, accepting the proposed standalone Pak packaging and scoped read-only launch diagnostics. This authorizes this scoped launcher migration and diagnostics; installation approval stays with the owner. Hardware deployment and the repair prompt follow validation.

Validation so far: old launcher fails the new standalone regression; 494 container tests across 33 binaries pass, with unchanged goldens. Final extra collision test, lint, device cross-build and independent review are running. Results will be recorded before merge.

author: otavio
body:
## Summary

Hardening from the 2026-11 audit, accepted as hardening (not an advisory) in shellhub-io/team#406. Two parts.

**A: the console can no longer be framed.** A page that frames the console could cover the SSH key approval screen and leave only its "Add key" button clickable under a decoy.

```diff
 ui/sws.toml  [**]                   # installs without the gateway
+  X-Frame-Options: DENY
+  Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'none'
 Caddyfile.tmpl  console handle      # replaces the console server's value, so each header appears once
+  header >X-Frame-Options "DENY"
+  header >Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'none'"
 Caddyfile.tmpl  TLS site only
+  header Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=31536000"   # no includeSubDomains
```

A full CSP for the SPA is a separate follow-up.

**B: the confirmation code guards the key binding.** Clicking "Add key" used to write the identity at once, and the code typed at the terminal only released the waiting connection.

```diff
 POST /api/ssh-approvals/:code/confirm
   decide approval (pending → confirmed)
-  write SSH identity for the approver
+  store the expiry the approver chose          # migration 059

 gateway ApprovalChallenge
   Confirm(typed code)                        # code must match the console's
   Resume
     authorize approver
+    RedeemSSHApproval(code, typed code)      # one tx: delete the confirmed row, write the identity
```

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Click "Add key" | Writes the identity | Records the approval |
| Code typed at the terminal | Releases the connection | Writes the identity and releases the connection |
| Approved, code never typed | Reconnecting works: the key is already an identity | Nothing is bound; connect again |

Confirm still answers 409 for a key that is already another member's identity. The console now says the key joins your identities once the terminal continues, instead of "Key added". The OpenAPI text and `login-approvals.mdx` say the key is bound when the code is typed.

## Evidence

- **Frame headers:** `TestTheConsoleRefusesToBeFramed` sends real requests through the gateway with a stub console that answers `SAMEORIGIN`. Before, the response had no frame headers. After, it has exactly one `DENY` and one `frame-ancestors 'none'`. Without the deferred `>`, it carried both values. static-web-server 2.44.2, run with this `sws.toml`, sends both headers.
- **HSTS:** `TestHTTPSTellsBrowsersToStayOnHTTPS` covers HTTPS, and `TestPlainHTTPSendsNoHSTS` covers plain HTTP.
- **Connect desktop app:** I checked it with a harness using Electron 34.5.8, the version Connect pins, and Connect's window settings (`webviewTag`, `persist:shellhub`, its CORS header rewrite). A page sending both headers loads in a `<webview>`, which is how Connect embeds the console, and is refused in an `<iframe>` (`ERR_BLOCKED_BY_RESPONSE`). Without the headers, both load.
- **Binding on the typed code:**
  - The store test checks that redeem needs a confirmed approval, the matching confirmation code, and an unexpired window, and works only once. Deleting the confirmation-code condition makes it fail.
  - The service tests check that confirm writes no identity and that redeem writes it with the approver's expiry.
  - The session tests check that `Resume` asks the access policy first, so a refused login (a member removed after approving, for one) binds nothing, and that a failed redeem refuses the login.
- **Redeem re-checks the approver:** an approver who left the namespace or lost the role to add SSH keys between confirming and typing the code binds nothing. If two connections with one key race to redeem for the same approver, the one that loses the insert retries and finds the identity already bound to that approver.
- **End to end:** the identity, approval, policy, reauth, revocation and API-key suites in `tests/` pass. The regression cases for the issue's acceptance criteria are in #7966, stacked on this PR: confirming without typing the code binds nothing, a reconnect before the code is typed is asked for approval again, and typing the code binds the key to the approver.

## Merge Danger

**Door:** one-way

Migration 059 adds a nullable `identity_expires_in` column to `ssh_approvals`. Rolling back runs its down migration. Approvals live for 90 s, so nothing is stranded.

**Blast Radius:** enrollment

- During a rolling upgrade, an approval confirmed by an old server and typed on a new gateway was already bound by the old server. Redeem then finds the key bound to the same account, so the login goes through.
- An approved key whose login the access policy refuses is no longer bound: the person approves again from a device the policy lets them reach. On master, confirming bound it whatever the policy said.
- A browser page that frames the console stops working. Nothing in our repos does this.
- HSTS makes browsers that visited over TLS stick to HTTPS on the console's host for a year.
- cloud: the paired branch only regenerates the store mock (shellhub-io/cloud, `fix/console-clickjacking-headers`).

Closes shellhub-io/team#406

body:
On a computer the message box had up to seven loose controls. `.attach-btn`, `.composer-emoji` and `.send-more` were centred while the rest sat at the bottom (and `.send-more`'s rule never applied, since the menu wraps it), so a second line of text split the row in two.

**The box**
- Every control is as tall as send and sits on the last line.
- **+ menu**: Upload a file (with the size limit), Poll (`pollCreate`), Sticker (`sendStickers`), each shown only where the chat's network takes it. Where files are all it takes (Matrix, Telegram, WhatsApp…), the + is a plain paperclip, so there is never a menu of one.
- Send and its menu (Send silently, Send later) are one button with a narrow right half.

**Making a poll**
- No dialog: the box turns into the poll's draft, shaped like the poll it becomes. The header names the network and its limits ("2 to 10 options"), with pills for One choice / Several, plus Open for on Discord (Signal has no timer).
- What the box held becomes the question. Enter moves down and sends from the last line; Esc or × goes back to the message with its text kept.

**Checked** against a demo hub in headless Chromium, on Discord #dev, a Signal group and a Matrix room: controls share one bottom at two lines, the + menu holds file/poll/sticker, the poll draft sends a 2-option poll on both networks and the box comes back empty, Esc keeps the text, and Matrix shows the paperclip alone, with no script errors. `verify-media-kinds` passes. author: bjacobso
body:
Ask 0015, item 3: a read-only option on the SQLite layer.

## What it adds

**`SqliteTriples.layerReadOnly({ filename })`** gives `Triples` over an existing SQLite file:

- The file is opened with the driver's `readonly` flag and `PRAGMA query_only = ON`, and WAL setup is skipped.
- No migration runs, because it uses the unmigrated adapter.
- Every write fails with `WriteError`.
- Acquisition checks the schema version first. Unless the file is at this release's version, it fails with **`SchemaVersionError`** (`expectedVersion`, `actualVersion`; zero for a file with no Triplex schema), the same typed error PostgreSQL's unmigrated layers already use.

**`SchemaVersionError` moves to `@triplex-build/triplex/sql`**, so SQLite and PostgreSQL share it. `/postgres` still exports it; it is the same class.

## Tests (`packages/sqlite/test/read-only.test.ts`)

- **A migrated file:** reads work, and a write fails with `WriteError`. The database file is byte-identical afterwards. SQLite still creates its shared-memory side files for a WAL-mode file, as documented, and the WAL stays empty.
- **A file one migration behind:** fails with `SchemaVersionError { expectedVersion: N, actualVersion: N-1 }`, and the file is not migrated.
- **A file with no Triplex schema:** `actualVersion: 0`.

## Docs and checks

- **Docs:** `docs/sqlite.md` describes the read-only layer, and `docs/host-integration.md` names the new export location.
- **Changeset:** minor.
- **Locally:** format, lint, typecheck, docs, tests and build pass, as do `pnpm pack:check` and PostgreSQL integration (86/86).

Las selecciones eran «solo mercado» (α = 0). No tenían modelo ni guardaban resultados, así que el sistema no veía un 7-0 o un 0-5 de visita. Tampoco había amistosos.

- **Modelo propio de selecciones** (`modelos/selecciones_modelo.py`):

author: finger563
body:
## Rocks on the ground

The first round of making the ground worth an away team. Every world with terrain is strewn with rock: boulders, stones and pebbles, placed over each terrain chunk as it is built, from the chunk's own height grid, so every rock sits on the triangles that are drawn (the drawn mesh and the full field part by metres on rough ground, which is why feet and skids already read the drawn mesh). Nothing is stored: a rock is a pure function of the planet and the chunk, so every visit puts every rock back where it was.

**Shapes.** `GroundRocks` builds four meshes once per process, like the asteroids in `RockMeshes`, but broken into the shapes rock takes on a planet: fractured talus (a dozen flat breaks at random angles), blocks jointed off bedded cliffs (three near-square joint sets, corners chipped), slabs a bed thick, and water-worn cobbles. An icosphere is planed by the breaks, normals split at the creases so a break reads as an edge, three LODs (the GPU picks each instance's by screen size), convex collision from the coarsest. Each mesh fills a unit box, so an instance's scale is the rock's size in metres and its burial depth is known.

**Where they lie.** `TerrainScatter` reads the fields the material paints with. Fans of boulders lie below the cliffs among the ones the refinement already raises in the height field; rockfall at the foot of a canyon wall, in the colour of the bed it fell from; cobbles along the river in the gorge; ejecta round the craters of the airless moons; pebble pavements on dry flats, few on wet ground. None under the snow, in the water, or inside a town on a world with settlements (the towns `SlonkCities` would build near the chunk, found the same way; a colony founded later, through `SetNightLights`, has its chunks' rocks rebuilt in place, the coarser chunk showing meanwhile). Density comes from the structure's slope through the refinement's own cliff, talus and flat regimes, which read the same at every level of the quadtree.

**Levels of detail.** Each size class has a lattice of candidates in cube-face coordinates nested in the quadtree, one hashed candidate per cell, so a rock a coarse chunk carries is carried again, at the same place, by the finer chunks that replace it on the way down; only its height settles onto the finer mesh. A class rides on the chunks fine enough to show it: boulders on chunks up to about 150 m across (seen to about 600 m), stones 40 m (150 m), pebbles the last level (35 m).

**Drawing them.** Each chunk gets an instanced static mesh per shape from a pool, attached to the chunk's mesh so the instances are chunk-relative (floats stay exact) and shown, hidden and released with the chunk. `M_GroundRock` lays the terrain's cliff texture set triplanar in the rock's own frame in centimetres of rock, so a pebble and a boulder have the same grain; the tint is the terrain's rock colour where the rock lies, varied per rock, and a canyon-wall rock picks its bed's colour with the terrain material's own hash so the two agree on the GPU. Snow lies on faces that look up.

**Standing on them.** Rocks 45 cm across and over within 40 m of the pawn get a collision-only copy on the boots' channel, rebuilt when the pawn has walked ten metres or the chunks round it change, and not at all for a craft racing over the ground. A transporter's destination has its rocks pinned solid for the length of the transport, so the arrival trace stands the person on a boulder rather than inside it. The crew's existing floor and wall traces do the rest: a low rock is stepped up onto, a big one walked round.


*Stills from play (a rock field on Meozaleth I; boulders on a test moon's sunlit ridge) to be attached here.*

### Performance

The planet turns every frame, and an instanced component that moves works its bounds out afresh from every one of its instances: at a hundred thousand rocks that was ten milliseconds of the game thread (33 fps against 63 with the rocks off, on Meozaleth I). The rocks are now a small `UInstancedStaticMeshComponent` subclass, `URockInstancesComponent`, that boxes its instances once in its own frame when they are set and moves the box, so its bounds hold every rock at O(1) per frame. (The engine's conservative bounds do the same but are only made when the instances reach the renderer, which a hidden chunk's rocks never do: 3 ms more.) Pooled components are detached so the turn no longer moves them. With about 97,000 rocks showing the frame is 15.8 ms against 12.5 ms with the rocks off, all on the game and render threads; the GPU sits at 6 ms. About 1,800 instance components accumulate in the pool; merging them is the next lever if those milliseconds matter.

### Code

- `GroundRocks.h/.cpp` (new): `EGroundRock`, the four meshes.
- `TerrainScatter.h/.cpp` (new): `FScatterSettings` and the palette, `SlonkScatter::ScatterChunk` on a chunk's grid, the classes, densities, shapes, sizes and tints.
- `PlanetTerrainComponent`: chunk builds take the scatter settings and return the chunk's rocks; the rock pool, `SetChunkVisible` for the mesh and its rocks together, the collision copies round the pawn, `SetScatterOptions`, the palette from the material parameters, `CheckSolidRocks`; `CubeDir` and `FaceUV` static, `GridHeightAt` shared with the ground queries, `ChunkAt` and `BuildChunkScatterForTest` for the tests.
- `PlanetBody`: tells the terrain whether the world has towns.
- `StarshipPawn`: `ship terrain rocks [on|off|density <x>|check]`; `check` traces the boots' channel down through the 40 solid rocks nearest the pawn.
- `tools/planet_materials/ground_rock_material.py` and `Content/Slonk/Materials/M_GroundRock.uasset` (new).
- `Tests/SlonkTerrainTests.cpp` (new), README (the rocks, the tests), `docs/testing.md`.

### Tests

`Slonk.Terrain.RocksNest`, `RocksGrounded` and `RocksTowns` build chunks as a chunk build does, without a world: a chunk and its four children carry the same boulders in the same place (27 of 27 and 110 of 110 on two rocky chunks), every rock is seated in the drawn ground and none is in the water (971 rocks, 508 of them pebbles), the same chunk carries the same rocks every time, and no rock is inside a town (none, against 13 with the rule off). The full suite passes, 35 of 35, run headless on Windows after the review fixes, with both targets built.

In play on Windows: on Meozaleth I, beamed down from 60 m and walked out, and on a 400 km moon from `ship spawnplanet moon 400` with the ship parked 300 m up; `ship terrain rocks check` found 40 of the 40 nearest solid rocks stopping the boots' trace on both.

### Not yet checked

- Not built on the Mac.
- A handled ensure fired once during play, in the renderer: a dynamic ray-tracing instance skipped because its geometry was evicted ("geometry 'None'"). Dynamic ray-tracing geometry here is the terrain's dynamic mesh chunks, not the rock instances; whether it predates this branch is not yet known.
- Rocks are kept out of towns but not off the roads between them, and a landed shuttle's skids can stand in a boulder.
